paras: The beating of Dillard Freeman was an assault on a Black worker in Lowndes County, Alabama, by three members of the Dixon family, whose brother, the county sheriff, was accused of holding Freeman and others as peons. By his own account to federal prosecutors in June 1903, he was dragged seven miles by a rope around his neck and whipped with a gin strap for visiting his mother without permission, then threatened with death if he testified truthfully. Carried in a Montgomery dispatch by white weeklies and Black papers, the case was offered as proof that peonage amounted to slavery.

In June 1903 a federal grand jury at Montgomery was investigating peonage, which a Montgomery dispatch said had been found in Tallapoosa, Coosa and Lowndes counties. The Lowndes sheriff, named only as Dixon, was accused of maintaining peons in addition to controlling the county's regularly convicted prisoners. He was one of five brothers who dominated county politics, "rough, violent men" against whom witnesses were "exceedingly difficult to obtain." The Montgomery Advertiser recorded Lowndes County witnesses, one white and one Black, before the grand jury on June 18 and 19, without naming the Dixons or Freeman.

Freeman had never been convicted of any offense; Dixon had ostensibly hired him at agreed wages under a contract that let Dixon treat him as a prisoner. Dixon told him they were "educating him to be a trusty."

At an unstated date, Freeman left the sheriff's place at Hayneville without permission to visit his mother, who lived seven miles away. The Dixons followed him to her cabin, forced their way in, took him outside and, in his mother's presence, beat him over the head with pistols. They tied a rope around his neck, fastened the other end to a horse and, with two brothers riding behind, marched him back to Hayneville; he had to keep his feet "or be strangled."

At Hayneville he was whipped with a gin strap across his bare back and legs by a man described as six feet tall and 250 pounds. Freeman lost consciousness after the fifteenth blow, and the dispatch cited testimony that the total was not less than a hundred. After he was subpoenaed, the brothers pursued him to the federal courthouse in Montgomery, and the brothers, one of them the sheriff, warned that he would be killed if he told the grand jury the truth.

Freeman told his story to U.S. District Attorney Warren S. Reese and his assistant, Sternfeldt, and was placed under the protection of the federal attorneys in Montgomery. The dispatch said Judge Thomas G. Jones would have punished the brothers quickly for the threat had corroborating proof been obtained. The coverage found does not report whether Freeman testified or whether any of the Dixons was charged.

The fullest text appeared on June 25 in the Union County Courier of Elk Point, South Dakota, under the headline "NEGRO SLAVERY DOWN IN ALABAMA" and the subhead "Dragged by a Rope." The same text ran on June 26 and 27 in South Dakota and Kansas weeklies; the Kansas Agitator titled it "HELD IN ABJECT SLAVERY," with the deck "Boys Tortured until nearly Dead for Running Away." The dispatch's own phrase, "peonage—slavery is a better word," set the line these papers followed. The Montgomery Advertiser's grand-jury reports did not name Freeman or the Dixons.

The Topeka Plaindealer printed the dispatch on its June 26 front page under the headline "Since Slavery Exists" and the deck "Slavery Exists in the South as it Did Forty Odd Years Ago." It introduced the text as one of the "chapters of horrors now appearing in the daily press" beside an editorial predicting that "Such will be the ultimate end of Negro peonage." The Sedalia Times reprinted the Plaindealer's selection on July 1, including its connecting line to the Tallapoosa cases. The Cleveland Gazette's condensed version, dated Montgomery, July 2, called the attackers "three men" and "his pursuers" and hedged with "It is alleged" and "he says."
The accounts differ only in detail: the Plaindealer gave Lowndes County's Black population as outnumbering whites "nearly two to one," where other copies said nearly ten to one.

reader.title: Beating of Dillard Freeman
bases: The dispatch presents the beating as punishment of a worker held under a contract letting the sheriff treat him 'as a prisoner' though never convicted, in a county where the sheriff was accused of maintaining peons (A5, A9, A21).

Every account of the beating is a version of one Montgomery dispatch resting on Freeman's statement to federal attorneys (A5, A7, A20); local Montgomery reports on the Lowndes witnesses do not name him or the Dixons (A1, A2).
